note.text: Tropical rainforests occur in warm humid parts of the tropics, including southern Cameroon and the wider Congo Basin, Amazonia and Southeast Asia. Broad-leaved trees form a canopy with emergents and shaded lower layers. Lianas and epiphytes use tree structure in different ways. Warmth and moisture often support rapid decomposition and nutrient cycling, while many strongly weathered soils retain limited readily available nutrients. Forest richness does not prove deep, uniformly fertile soil. Rainfall seasonality varies within the broad rainforest category.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to connect year-round moisture and warmth to forest structure and interpret a model rainfall chart. Builds on: ecosystem functioning and nutrient cycling. Leads to: comparison with seasonal savannah and monsoon landscapes.

sections.heading: Explain the geography

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: Southern Cameroon supplies a local setting for comparing forest cover, cultivation and conservation. Farming and logging can provide livelihoods but alter habitat, canopy and nutrient pathways; outcomes depend on methods and intensity. The chart is an invented warm-region rainfall record with moisture in every month, not measured data for Douala or a test proving rainforest from rainfall alone.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Explain a link: shade affects understorey growth; continuous moisture supports growth and decomposition; clearing changes both habitat and soil exposure. Distinguish a liana rooted in soil from an epiphyte growing on a plant for support. Read seasonality before adding monthly totals and state the limits of the model.

cards.idea: Distinguish the features before applying them.
example: canopy structure: overlapping forest layers influencing light below.
rapid nutrient cycling: relatively quick transfer through litter decomposition and plant uptake in warm moist conditions.
epiphyte: a plant growing on another plant for support without being defined as a parasite.
land-use impact: change in forest structure and processes caused by human activity.

cards.idea: Use the evidence in the example, not a place name alone.
example: Tall crowns shade a lower layer of the model forest.
Litter breaks down and plants take up released nutrients.
An orchid grows on a tree branch while obtaining resources from its surroundings.
Clearing alters shade, habitat and the supply of litter.

cards.idea: Explain how the process produces the stated effect.
example: Canopy interception creates differences in light between layers.
Large nutrient stores can be in vegetation and cycling material rather than a rich enduring soil store.
Support and parasitism are different relationships.
Removing cover and biomass changes more than the number of visible trees.

questions.prompt: Read the invented monthly rainfall chart. Add the labels above all monthly bars to obtain the annual total in mm; the vertical-axis tick labels are not extra observations.

misconceptions.explain: That is a monthly mean, not the sum for the year.
That is the difference between wettest and driest months, not the annual total.
That multiplies an already millimetre total by ten without a unit conversion.

solution: The annual rainfall of this classroom record is {answer} mm. A real biome classification also needs temperature and other evidence.

right.text: canopy structure: overlapping forest layers influencing light below.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: Canopy interception creates differences in light between layers. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

right.text: rapid nutrient cycling: relatively quick transfer through litter decomposition and plant uptake in warm moist conditions.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: Large nutrient stores can be in vegetation and cycling material rather than a rich enduring soil store. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

right.text: epiphyte: a plant growing on another plant for support without being defined as a parasite.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: Support and parasitism are different relationships. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

right.text: land-use impact: change in forest structure and processes caused by human activity.
right.explain: This distinction is correct: Removing cover and biomass changes more than the number of visible trees. Look for a claim that reverses the process or makes an unsupported generalisation.

wrong.text: All rainforest plants receive the same light at ground level.
wrong.explain: Canopy interception creates differences in light between layers.

wrong.text: High forest biomass proves every nutrient remains permanently in topsoil.
wrong.explain: Large nutrient stores can be in vegetation and cycling material rather than a rich enduring soil store.

wrong.text: Every plant using a tree for support must feed parasitically on it.
wrong.explain: Support and parasitism are different relationships.

wrong.text: Clearing cannot change erosion exposure or ecosystem processes.
wrong.explain: Removing cover and biomass changes more than the number of visible trees.
